items.title: NSA FOIA Records Detail Pentagon’s 1992 Search for Answers on Missing Cold War Aircrews
items.summary: Records released by the National Security Agency to The Black Vault in September 2025, and now being published online by The Black Vault, provide additional details about a 1992 Pentagon effort to examine Cold War reconnaissance losses and determine whether missing American personnel may have fallen into the hands of the Soviet Union, China or North Korea. The records include historical summaries of U.S. reconnaissance incidents and aircraft losses, along with a June 1992 memorandum concerning a Joint Staff effort to examine Cold War POW/MIA cases. Much of the history of the underlying reconnaissance incidents has been documented previously. The significance of the material is instead found in the internal Pentagon discussion surrounding those losses and the questions officials were examining decades later. Among the most notable passages is a statement that, for some losses, the government’s “official” explanation and what actually happened could represent “two different stories.” The documents do not establish that missing U.S. servicemen survived in foreign custody. Nor do they establish that official explanations for particular aircraft losses were false. They document questions Pentagon officials were examining in 1992, and some portions of which remain classified today. items.title: FOI lawsuits on origins of Covid-19,  gain-of-function research and biolabs
items.summary: U.S. Right to Know, a nonprofit newsroom and public health research group, has filed 46 lawsuits against federal and state agencies for violating Freedom of Information laws. The lawsuits are part of our efforts to uncover what is known about the origins of novel coronavirus SARS-CoV-2, leaks or mishaps at biosafety labs, and the risks of gain-of-function research that seeks to augment the infectivity or lethality of potential pandemic pathogens. We have filed 298 state, federal, and international public records requests seeking information about the origins of SARS-CoV-2, and the risks of biosafety labs and gain-of-function research. Read more about our findings so far , why we are conducting this investigation , recommended readings and documents we have obtained in our investigations. The lawsuit, filed in U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, seeks cable traffic between the State Department and the American Institute in Taiwan (AIT Taipei) that relates to Taiwanese data or assessments about the origins of the COVID-19 pandemic. Case 3:26-cv-08558. (45) Department of Energy: On April 28, 2026, USRTK filed a lawsuit against the DOE for violating provisions of the FOIA. items.title: CIA Release Reveals Internal Bin Laden Raid Talking Points, Q&A and Declassification Records
items.summary: A newly obtained Central Intelligence Agency release provides a detailed look at the material prepared inside the U.S. government for the public rollout following the May 2011 raid that killed Osama bin Laden, including internal talking points, an extensive question-and-answer package, public-affairs guidance and records documenting the expedited declassification of intelligence imagery. The 35-page responsive record was provided by the CIA in response to a Freedom of Information Act request filed by The Black Vault with the agency in August 2013. In its July 6, 2026, final response, the CIA said it had located the document in its “database of previously-released records” after determining that an earlier FOIA request had sought records on the same subject. Searches conducted for this article, however, did not locate the complete document in the CIA’s online Electronic Reading Room or elsewhere through conventional web searches. Some portions may therefore be newly accessible online through this release, although that cannot be fully established. What can be established is that this newly obtained package brings together internal records showing how that information was prepared, cleared and organized for public disclosure. CIA Withholds Records About What Happened to Bin Laden’s Body The FOIA request contained two separate items. While the CIA released a previously processed record (at least, in part) responsive to the second, it refused to release records responsive to the…

Often dubbed “Pennsylvania’s Roswell,” it involved reports of a fiery fireball streaking over several U.S. states and Canada, a crash in the woods near the village of Kecksburg, and an alleged military recovery of an unknown object [1] . Over the decades, the incident has been the subject of intense speculation – from meteor to secret Cold War satellite to extraterrestrial craft – and persistent efforts by investigators to unearth official records. This deep dive examines all angles of the Kecksburg case, drawing on eyewitness accounts, media reports, and released government documents (many obtained via The Black Vault’s FOIA requests) to present a balanced, evidence-backed picture of what we know. items.title: The Pangram Paradox: The Problem with AI “Detecting” other AIs
items.summary: Op-ed: This is an opinion piece published on Unlimited Hangout . Most articles published on UH are not opinion pieces, so we are clearly labeling those that are. It should be no secret to readers of Unlimited Hangout that I have a very negative view of the impact that Artificial Intelligence (AI) is having on independent media and media in general. As someone who has been impersonated by AI daily on large video platforms for a few years now, I have come to acutely feel that AI is becoming a dangerous force that is making it increasingly difficult for well-meaning readers/viewers to distinguish between what is real and what is false. I don’t mean just for those hoping to view my content, as the personal issue I am facing is a microcosm of a much larger problem. As a result, one might think that I would have been pleased, if not relieved, to see Substack, a large platform for professional writers, partner with an “AI detection tool.” Not only am I not pleased, but I have now taken the time to write an opinion piece explaining why I think this is bad and to also explain where I think a lot of this is going. Substack’s new partner and, apparently, the AI detection tool of choice for most major media outlets right now is called Pangram. Pangram was founded in 2023, originally under the name Checkfor.ai, by Max Spero and Bradley Emi. The documents are posted below in approximately the chronological order in which we received them. We have filed 305 state, federal, and international public records requests, and 46 FOI lawsuits , seeking information about the origins of SARS-CoV-2 and the risks of biosafety labs and gain-of-function research. As of September 1, 2026, U.S. Right to Know has obtained and published more than 280,000 pages of public records related to COVID-19 origins, gain-of-function research and biosafety. In July 2020, U.S. Right to Know began submitting public records requests in pursuit of data from public institutions in an effort to discover what is known about the origins of the novel coronavirus SARS-CoV-2, which causes the disease Covid-19. We are also researching accidents, leaks and other mishaps at laboratories where pathogens of pandemic potential are stored and modified, and the risks of gain-of-function research, which involve experiments on such pathogens to increase their host range, infectivity, transmissibility or pathogenicity. items.title: Larry W. Bryant and the CIA: UFO Investigations, FOIA Disputes, and Government Correspondence
items.summary: Larry W. Bryant was a UFO researcher, writer, and government transparency advocate who pursued federal records through the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA). His work included efforts to obtain documents concerning unidentified flying objects, intelligence activities, and government accountability. Bryant also contributed to UFO Magazine, where he examined government records and controversies involving UFO research. His correspondence with the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) provides a historical record of his efforts to obtain information and challenge agency disclosure decisions. This collection, released by the CIA under FOIA case F-2021-02420, contains historical correspondence, administrative records, appeals, and other materials associated with Bryant’s dealings with the agency. Among the subjects addressed are UFO investigations, alleged intelligence operations, and disputes over the CIA’s handling of information requests. The documents include correspondence concerning the agency’s searches, withholding decisions, fee assessments, and Bryant’s attempts to obtain recognition as a representative of the news media. One notable portion concerns Bryant’s efforts to obtain records associated with the November 1986 Japan Airlines UFO encounter over Alaska and a subsequent meeting reportedly held at Federal Aviation Administration headquarters in 1987. His correspondence with the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) provides a historical record of his efforts to obtain information and challenge agency disclosure decisions. This collection, released by the CIA under FOIA case F-2021-02420, contains historical correspondence, administrative records, appeals, and other materials associated with Bryant’s dealings with the agency. Among the subjects addressed are UFO investigations, alleged intelligence operations, and disputes over the CIA’s handling of information requests. The documents include correspondence concerning the agency’s searches, withholding decisions, fee assessments, and Bryant’s attempts to obtain recognition as a representative of the news media. One notable portion concerns Bryant’s efforts to obtain records associated with the November 1986 Japan Airlines UFO encounter over Alaska and a subsequent meeting reportedly held at Federal Aviation Administration headquarters in 1987.
